# Welcome! {.unnumbered}

This page accompanies the practical session on *biomarker discovery from
expression data* (Wednesday, 7 October 2026, 14:45–16:00) of the EMBO
Practical Course
[Causality in Biomedicine](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/training/events/causality-in-biomedicine-2026/).

Earlier today, you heard two lectures: one on causal effects of *shifting* a
continuous exposure (applied to immune correlates of protection in vaccine
trials), and one on biomarker discovery with causal inference and machine
learning (`biotmle`). This session revisits the key ideas of both lectures,
hands-on. Neither `R` package is on the course VM, so instead we will **build
each method from its parts**: you have all of the pieces from earlier in the
week (structural causal models, identification, model misspecification,
targeted learning).

## The two parts

1. [**Biomarker discovery as causal effect estimation.**](chapters/biotmle.qmd)
   Which CpG sites in whole blood are affected by smoking? We will
   reconstruct the `biotmle` procedure: an efficient, machine-learning-based
   estimator of the average treatment effect (ATE) for each CpG, combined
   with the variance moderation that makes `limma` so useful in high
   dimensions. Real data from @su2016distinct, as analyzed in
   @hejazi2017generalization.
2. [**Stochastic-interventional vaccine efficacy (SVE).**](chapters/sve.qmd)
   How would vaccine efficacy change if a vaccine induced higher (or lower)
   antibody titers? We will estimate the effect of *shifting* an immune
   marker, in a simulated vaccine trial with a case-cohort design.

A theme runs through both: each causal parameter we target **reduces to a
familiar coefficient of a linear model** when that model is correct. The
linear model is more accessible, but more brittle — and the exercises ask
you to see exactly where it breaks.

In Part 1, the biomarker is an *outcome* of the exposure; in Part 2, the
biomarker lies *on the causal pathway* between vaccination and infection —
it is a mediator, and the SVE asks what happens when we intervene on it.

## How the session works

- ~5 min: introduction.
- ~30 min: Part 1, then ~5 min going over the answers together.
- ~25 min: Part 2, then ~5 min going over the answers together.
- ~5 min: wrap-up.

Exercises come in two kinds:

- ✏️ **pen and paper**: short derivations or explanations, and
- 💻 **coding**: fill in the blanks (`___`) in the code
  provided, then run it.

Work in pairs if you like. Nima, Sjoerd, and the other instructors will be
circulating — please ask questions! Exercises marked *stretch* are for those
who finish early.

## Setup

All code runs on the course VM. Open RStudio, start a new script, and run:

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| eval: false
library(SuperLearner)
library(lmtp)
library(ggplot2)

# helper functions and data for this session
source("practical/R/moderate.R")
source("practical/R/sim_vaccine_trial.R")
methy <- read.csv("practical/data/su2016_methylation.csv.gz")
```

The data and helper scripts can also be downloaded directly:
[`su2016_methylation.csv.gz`](practical/data/su2016_methylation.csv.gz),
[`moderate.R`](practical/R/moderate.R),
[`sim_vaccine_trial.R`](practical/R/sim_vaccine_trial.R).
